doctrines.question: Did God create the universe out of nothing by a free act, or does the created order emerge from pre-existing matter?
doctrines.framing: Every historic confession that addresses origins agrees that God made the universe out of nothing, by a free act of his will, not by shaping matter that already existed or by any necessity in his own nature. This is affirmed alike by the Fourth Lateran Council, the Nicene Creed's confession of God as maker of heaven and earth, and Westminster's opening chapter on creation; no branch of the historic church has ever taught that matter is eternal or that the universe flows of necessity from the divine essence. The genuinely open question in this domain is not whether God made the world but how the order and apparent design within it are best discerned, a question the doctrines below take up.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places creation ex nihilo at T1.5, just below the first tier: it is confessed everywhere but does not itself divide on the gospel the way T1 doctrines do.

open.todo: Work out how to speak carefully about design in creation without overclaiming what an argument can establish, since creation out of nothing itself is not actually in question.

positions.label: Creation ex nihilo
positions.hold: God created the universe out of nothing, by a free act of his will, not from pre-existing matter and not by any necessity in his own nature.
positions.why: Scripture presents God speaking the universe into being and calling into existence the things that do not exist, and the historic creeds confess him as maker of all things visible and invisible.
positions.vs: Treating matter as eternal and uncreated, or treating the universe as an emanation flowing of necessity from the divine nature rather than as a free act of will.

doctrines.question: What kind of literature is Genesis 1, and what follows from reading it that way?
doctrines.framing: Genesis 1 can be read as straightforward historical narrative describing six ordinary days, as a literary framework organizing creation topically rather than chronologically, as an analogy in which each day pictures a longer period, as an account of God assigning functions within a cosmic temple, or as a text that uses and subverts the creation language of surrounding ancient Near Eastern cultures. These are judgments about the kind of text Genesis 1 is, not conclusions about modern science, and the reading taken here does not by itself settle the age of the earth or the mechanism behind the diversity of life, which are treated as separate questions below.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places the genre question at the third tier: it governs how the rest of this domain is read without itself dividing on the gospel.

open.todo: Work out which genre judgment for Genesis 1 is exegetically strongest, since that reading shapes how the age-of-the-earth and evolution questions below are approached.

positions.label: Historical narrative
positions.hold: Genesis 1 is straightforward historical narrative, describing God's creation of the universe and all it contains across six ordinary, sequential days.
positions.why: The chapter uses ordinary Hebrew narrative verb forms and numbers each day with the formula evening and morning, the same construction Exodus later treats as the pattern for the ordinary work week.
positions.vs: Reading the days of Genesis 1 as a topical framework, a long-age analogy, or a temple-inauguration account rather than as an ordinary sequence of days.

held_by.note: The statement says: “The days in Genesis do not correspond to geologic ages but are six consecutive, 24-hour days of creation.” A young-earth reading is common within the tradition's more conservative wing, though the Baptist Faith and Message does not itself specify.
held_by.citation: Answers in Genesis, Statement of Faith, “Origins and History” section

held_by.note: The statement says: “The Bible is the written Word of God, and because it is inspired throughout, all its assertions are historically and scientifically true in the original autographs. To the student of nature this means that the account of origins in Genesis is a factual presentation of simple historical truths.” See the tradition override below for how this position relates to the cosmic-temple reading within the same stream.
held_by.citation: Creation Research Society, Statement of Belief, point 1

held_by.note: The homily reasons that Scripture says “one day” rather than “the first day” in order to fix the measure of day and night together: “Now twenty-four hours fill up the space of one day — we mean of a day and of a night.” Basil reads the day as ordinary time; other Fathers, including Origen, read the days non-literally, and no Orthodox council has dogmatized the question.
held_by.citation: Basil of Caesarea, Hexaemeron, Homily 2.8 (on Genesis 1:5)

positions.learn_detail: Held across several evangelical traditions less through confessional requirement than through parachurch statements of faith such as Answers in Genesis and the Creation Research Society, which individual members subscribe to personally.

positions.label: Framework view
positions.hold: Genesis 1 is arranged as a literary framework of two matching triads of days, organizing creation topically by forming and filling rather than narrating a strict chronological sequence.
positions.why: The days pair by theme, days one through three forming realms and days four through six filling them, a structure that signals topical arrangement rather than a bare chronological report.
positions.vs: Reading the six days as a strict chronological sequence rather than as a topical, two-triad literary structure.

held_by.note: See the tradition override below for how this relates to the analogical day-age reading within the same tradition.
held_by.citation: Meredith G. Kline, 'Space and Time in the Genesis Cosmogony,' Perspectives on Science and Christian Faith 48 (1996)

sources.label: Space and Time in the Genesis Cosmogony

positions.label: Analogical / day-age
positions.hold: Each day of Genesis 1 corresponds analogically to God's own day of work, a pattern given for the human week, without fixing how long each corresponding period of creation itself actually took.
positions.why: The Hebrew word for day already carries a range of senses elsewhere in Scripture, and Genesis 1 presents God's work week as a pattern for the human week rather than as a strict claim about elapsed time.
positions.vs: Treating the length of each creation day as a settled, literal twenty-four hours rather than as a question the text itself leaves analogical.

held_by.note: The OPC's report on the days of creation concluded that several readings, including this one, fall within the bounds of the Westminster Standards.
held_by.citation: OPC General Assembly, Report of the Committee to Study the Views of Creation Days (2000)

held_by.note: Rome does not require a literal six-day reading.
held_by.citation: Catechism of the Catholic Church, 283; Pius XII, Providentissimus Deus and Divino Afflante Spiritu on non-literal exegetical method

sources.label: Genesis 1-4: A Linguistic, Literary, and Theological Commentary

positions.label: Cosmic temple
positions.hold: Genesis 1 describes God assigning functions and taking up rest and rule within a cosmic temple, using the ancient world's temple-inauguration pattern rather than describing the material manufacture of the universe.
positions.why: The seven-day structure and God's rest on the seventh day match ancient Near Eastern temple-dedication accounts, in which a deity takes up rest and rule within a completed sanctuary.
positions.vs: Reading Genesis 1 as an account of the material origin of matter itself rather than as an account of functional order and divine rule within an already-existing cosmos.

held_by.note: See the tradition override below for how this relates to the historical-narrative reading within the same stream.
held_by.citation: John H. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (2009)

sources.label: The Lost World of Genesis One

positions.label: Ancient polemic
positions.hold: Genesis 1 is written to confront the creation accounts of surrounding ancient Near Eastern cultures, presenting the God of Israel alone as sovereign over a cosmos other nations attributed to rival gods.
positions.why: Genesis 1's ordering of sun, moon, sea and sea creatures directly counters deities Israel's neighbors worshipped under those same names, framing the chapter as polemic against surrounding religion.
positions.vs: Reading Genesis 1 as written primarily to answer a modern scientific question about material origins rather than as a polemic against the religious claims of Israel's neighbors.
positions.learn_detail: This reading is usually combined with one of the other four rather than standing alone as a complete account of the chapter's genre; no registered tradition confesses it by itself as a formal position.

sources.label: The Evolution of Adam

doctrines.learn_note: These five readings are not always mutually exclusive in practice; the cosmic-temple and ancient-polemic readings in particular are frequently combined with each other or with the framework view.

non-denominational.hold: Genesis 1's genre is not settled within non-denominational evangelicalism: some congregations read it as straightforward historical narrative describing six ordinary days, while others, following the cosmic-temple reading, read it as an account of functional order tied to temple-inauguration language.
non-denominational.note: Independent congregations vary widely and hold no binding confession on the question; position typically follows a congregation's teachers rather than a denominational standard.
non-denominational.citation: Creation Research Society, Statement of Belief, contrasted with John H. Walton, The Lost World of Genesis One (2009)

reformed.hold: Confessionally Reformed churches permit more than one reading of Genesis 1's genre: some hold the framework view associated with Meredith Kline, others the analogical day-age reading, and Reformed assemblies have generally declined to bind the conscience beyond affirming God's work of creation itself.
reformed.note: The Orthodox Presbyterian Church's 2000 study committee concluded that several views, including these two, fall within the bounds of the Westminster Standards.
reformed.citation: OPC General Assembly, Report of the Committee to Study the Views of Creation Days (2000)

doctrines.question: How old are the earth and the universe?
doctrines.framing: Geology, cosmology and the biblical genealogies have each been read to yield very different ages for the earth and the universe, from thousands of years to roughly fourteen billion. No historic confession specifies an age for the earth, so the dispute among traditions holding a high view of biblical authority is exegetical and scientific rather than creedal, though it is argued with real intensity on every side. This doctrine is closely linked to how Genesis 1's genre is read and to how the flood is understood, since a young earth and a global, geology-shaping flood are usually argued together.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places the age of the earth at the third tier: it is argued intensely but does not itself divide on the gospel.

open.todo: Work out whether the biblical genealogies and the genre of Genesis 1 require a young earth, or whether an old-earth or evolutionary-creationist reading is exegetically sound, and how far that judgment should be shaped by the scientific evidence either way.

positions.label: Young-earth creationism
positions.hold: The earth and universe are young, on the order of thousands rather than billions of years old, consistent with a straightforward reading of the biblical genealogies and the six ordinary days of Genesis 1.
positions.why: Genesis 1 read as ordinary days, joined to the genealogies from Adam to Abraham, yields a young chronology, and evidence such as rapid geological processes and soft tissue recovered from dinosaur fossils is read as consistent with a recent creation and a global flood that reshaped the earth's surface.
positions.vs: Treating the standard geological and cosmological timescales of billions of years as more authoritative than a straightforward reading of Genesis's days and genealogies.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Whether the earth is young is a live and sharp dispute among traditions holding a high view of biblical authority; no ecumenical creed specifies an age for the earth, so the dispute is exegetical and scientific rather than creedal.

held_by.note: The statement says: “Scripture teaches a recent origin of man and the whole creation, with history spanning approximately 4,000 years from creation to Christ.” Widely held within the tradition's more conservative wing; the Baptist Faith and Message does not itself specify an age.
held_by.citation: Answers in Genesis, Statement of Faith, “Origins and History” section

held_by.note: The statement affirms the Genesis account of origins as “a factual presentation of simple historical truths,” the basis for the society's young-earth chronology. See the tradition override below.
held_by.citation: Creation Research Society, Statement of Belief, point 1

held_by.note: Confessionally held within the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod; other Lutheran bodies do not require a young-earth reading.

positions.label: Old-earth creationism
positions.hold: The earth and universe are billions of years old, as indicated by geological and astronomical evidence, while Genesis 1 is read in a way that does not require a young chronology, and God creates directly and specially, including a historical Adam, without evolutionary common descent.
positions.why: The days of Genesis 1 need not be ordinary twenty-four-hour periods, and reading them in one of the text's other defensible genres removes any need to reconcile a young chronology with the converging evidence of radiometric dating, starlight travel time and the geological column.
positions.vs: Requiring a young chronology of thousands of years as the only reading faithful to Genesis 1, or extending old-earth findings into evolutionary common descent for living things.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Old-earth creationism sits between young-earth creationism and evolutionary creationism and is regarded by critics on each side as either compromising the text or resisting the evidence; no ecumenical creed specifies an age for the earth.

held_by.citation: OPC General Assembly, Report of the Committee to Study the Views of Creation Days (2000)

positions.label: Evolutionary creationism
positions.hold: The earth and universe are billions of years old and God brought about the diversity of life, including the human body, through the ordinary means of an evolutionary process he sovereignly directs and sustains, rather than by successive acts of special creation.
positions.why: The converging evidence of genetics, paleontology and geology for an old earth and common descent is read as a true account of how God exercised his ordinary providence, in the same way Scripture attributes the ordinary growth of an embryo to God's own hand.
positions.vs: Treating an evolutionary mechanism as incompatible with God's sovereign, purposeful creating, or requiring successive acts of special creation for each form of life.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Evolutionary creationism is disputed sharply within evangelicalism over how far common descent, including for the human body, can be affirmed without compromising the historicity of Adam and the fall Scripture presupposes; the position itself intends no denial of a historical Adam or the fall, though critics dispute whether the two are compatible in practice.

held_by.note: BioLogos affirms evolution, including common descent, as the best scientific explanation for the diversity of life over billions of years, held together with a Christ-centered, biblical faith (“Rigorous Science” and “Christ-centered Faith” among its three stated core values). doctrines.question: Did the diversity of life, including the human body, come about through a process of evolutionary common descent, or through direct acts of special creation?
doctrines.framing: Genesis describes God making each kind of living thing and forming the first man from the dust of the ground, while biology describes converging genetic and fossil evidence for common descent across living things, including humans. The disagreement is over whether that biological evidence describes the actual means God used, including for the human body, or whether it should be set aside in favor of a straightforward reading of Genesis's kinds and the forming of Adam. This mechanism question is distinct from, though closely tied to, the age-of-the-earth question above.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places evolution at the third tier: it is argued with real intensity but does not itself divide on the gospel.

open.todo: Work out whether the evidence for common descent, including for the human body, is strong enough to accept alongside a historical Adam and a real fall, or whether special creation of each kind is the more faithful reading.

positions.label: Special creation
positions.hold: God created each kind of living thing, including the human body, by a direct, discrete act rather than through evolutionary common descent from earlier life forms.
positions.why: Genesis repeatedly describes God making each kind of plant and animal according to its kind, and the man's body is formed directly from the dust of the ground rather than being described as the modified descendant of an earlier species.
positions.vs: Holding that the human body, along with other forms of life, descended by an evolutionary process from earlier, non-human ancestors.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Whether the human body specifically must be specially created, rather than descended by an evolutionary process God directed, is a live and sharp dispute among traditions holding a high view of biblical authority; no ecumenical creed addresses the biological mechanism of creation.

held_by.note: The statement says: “The various original life forms (kinds), including mankind, were made by direct, supernatural, creative acts of God (i.e., not by natural, physical processes over millions of years).” Widely held within the tradition's more conservative wing.
held_by.citation: Answers in Genesis, Statement of Faith, “Origins and History” section

held_by.note: Confessionally held within the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod.
held_by.citation: Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod, A Statement of Scriptural and Confessional Principles (1973)

positions.label: Evolutionary creationism
positions.hold: God brought about the diversity of life, including the human body, through the ordinary means of a directed evolutionary process of common descent, while specially creating each human person's soul and standing before him.
positions.why: The genetic, fossil and comparative-anatomical evidence for common descent is read as a true account of the ordinary means God used, in keeping with a God who works through, rather than only apart from, the processes he sustains.
positions.vs: Requiring a direct, discrete act of special creation for the human body rather than an evolutionary process God directs and sustains.
positions.orthodoxy_note: This position is disputed by traditions and individuals who hold that special creation of the human body is required by Genesis 2 and by the theological weight the fall places on a historical Adam; it is held here as compatible with, not a denial of, a historical Adam and a real fall.

doctrines.question: Was the flood of Noah's day a literal global catastrophe, a real but regional catastrophe, or an account whose purpose is primarily theological?
doctrines.framing: Genesis 6-9 narrates a flood sent as judgment on human sin, from which Noah's family and the animals aboard the ark were preserved. The disagreement is over the catastrophe's geographic scale, whether it covered the entire globe or was a real but regional event described in the universal idiom of its ancient audience, and over how much weight the narrative's theological purpose, judgment and covenant, should carry relative to a claim about the catastrophe's physical scale. This doctrine is usually argued together with the age of the earth, since a global flood is the primary mechanism young-earth creationism uses to account for the geological column.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places the flood at the third tier, alongside the age of the earth it is usually argued with.

open.todo: Work out whether Genesis 6-9's universal language requires a geographically global flood or is describing a regional catastrophe in the idiom of its ancient audience, and how that judgment relates to the reading taken on the age of the earth.

positions.label: Global flood
positions.hold: The flood of Noah's day was a literal, historical, worldwide catastrophe that covered the entire globe, including the highest mountains, reshaping the earth's geology and destroying all air-breathing land life outside the ark.
positions.why: Genesis repeatedly uses universal language, describing all the high mountains under the whole heaven as covered, and the flood narrative's scope and stated duration match a global rather than local catastrophe.
positions.vs: Reading the flood's universal language as describing a geographically local or regional event rather than a worldwide catastrophe.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Whether the flood covered the entire globe is a live and sharp dispute closely tied to the age-of-the-earth dispute above; no ecumenical creed specifies the flood's geographic extent.

held_by.note: The statement says: “The great flood of Genesis was an actual historic event, worldwide (global) in its extent and catastrophic in its effects. At one stage during the flood, the waters covered the entire surface of the whole globe.” Widely held within the tradition's more conservative wing.
held_by.citation: Answers in Genesis, Statement of Faith, “Origins and History” section

positions.label: Regional flood
positions.hold: The flood of Noah's day was a real, historical, catastrophic flood confined to the region of Noah's world, described in Genesis using the universal language ancient narrators used for a locally total catastrophe.
positions.why: The Hebrew word for earth or land in the flood narrative can denote the known regional world rather than the entire globe, and reading it that way matches how flood accounts elsewhere in the ancient Near East describe a locally total catastrophe in universal terms.
positions.vs: Requiring the flood to have covered the entire globe rather than the whole of the world as Noah and his contemporaries knew it.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Whether the flood was regional rather than global is disputed by traditions holding that the text's universal language requires a worldwide event; no ecumenical creed specifies the flood's geographic extent.

positions.label: Theological narrative
positions.hold: The flood account's primary purpose is theological rather than a claim about the catastrophe's scale: it recounts God's judgment on sin and his gracious preservation of a remnant, using ancient flood-narrative conventions Genesis reworks around its own theology.
positions.why: Genesis 6-9 shares structural parallels with Mesopotamian flood accounts such as Gilgamesh's, and its distinctive emphases, one righteous God, judgment for moral sin, an unconditional covenant, are what the narrative is actually written to establish.
positions.vs: Treating the flood narrative's primary purpose as settling a scientific or geographic question about the catastrophe's scale rather than as a theological account of judgment and covenant.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Read in a form that treats the narrative's historical referent as secondary or absent, this position is disputed by traditions holding that the flood, like the rest of Genesis, describes an event that actually happened; held here in a form that affirms a real historical event while locating the text's main purpose in its theology.
positions.learn_detail: Held by scholars across several traditions rather than as a confessional position of any registered tradition; usually combined with either the global or regional reading rather than replacing a judgment about historicity altogether.

doctrines.question: How should the miracles reported in Scripture be understood in relation to scientific inquiry into nature?
doctrines.framing: Scripture reports miracles, particular divine acts within nature, from the plagues of Egypt to the resurrection of Christ. Nearly every tradition affirms these as real events; the live questions are how such an account relates to a scientific method built to describe nature's ordinary regularities, and whether every miracle account in Scripture should be read as reporting an event that happened as narrated. The bodily resurrection of Christ is treated as settled elsewhere in this map; the question here concerns miracle claims and scientific method more generally.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places miracles and science at the second tier: it shapes how Scripture and science are held together without itself dividing on the gospel.

open.todo: Work out how far a scientific account of nature's regularities should shape confidence in a particular miracle claim, and whether any miracle account other than the resurrection is better read as theological shaping than as straightforward historical report.

positions.label: Real divine acts
positions.hold: Miracles are real, particular acts of God within his ordinarily ordered creation, neither violations of a self-sufficient nature nor beyond the reach of a God who freely sustains the natural order he made.
positions.why: Scripture presents God's miracles, culminating in the bodily resurrection of Christ, as real events within history and nature, consistent with a God who freely governs the order he continually sustains rather than a deity bound by it.
positions.vs: Treating the miraculous as either scientifically impossible in principle or as merely a symbolic idiom for events that did not actually occur.

positions.label: Methodological naturalism
positions.hold: The scientific method, by its own nature, investigates only natural causes and mechanisms and is therefore neither equipped to confirm nor to rule out a genuine miracle, which lies outside its proper competence rather than being disproved by it.
positions.why: Science proceeds by describing repeatable natural regularities, and a genuinely singular act of God is by definition not a repeatable natural regularity, so its absence from a scientific account says nothing about whether it occurred.
positions.vs: Treating the silence or limits of scientific method on a particular event as evidence against a miracle claim, when the method is not equipped to adjudicate the question either way.

held_by.note: BioLogos states “Rigorous Science” as one of three core values — affirming the established findings of modern science — held together with “Christ-centered Faith” upholding the authority of Scripture, rather than treating scientific method as competent to adjudicate a miracle claim either way. The page was rewritten in 2024 into a shorter statement; the corpus's earlier “articles 1-12” numbering no longer applies.
held_by.citation: BioLogos, Faith Commitments (2024 revision of “What We Believe”)

positions.learn_detail: This position is usually held together with, rather than as a rival to, the affirmation that miracles are real divine acts; it addresses what science as a method can and cannot adjudicate, not whether miracles occur.

positions.label: Theological, not historical
positions.hold: Scripture's miracle accounts are best read as conveying theological truth about God's power and presence rather than as reports of events that occurred exactly as narrated, with the account's meaning carried by its theological claim rather than by the event's historicity.
positions.why: Ancient religious narrative regularly conveys truth through symbol and theological shaping rather than through modern historical reportage, and reading miracle accounts this way removes any need to reconcile them with a scientific account of nature's regularities.
positions.vs: Requiring that a miracle account be read as reporting an event that occurred exactly as narrated in order for the account to be true and authoritative.
positions.orthodoxy_note: Applied to miracles generally this is a live methodological dispute; applied to the bodily resurrection of Christ specifically it moves outside what the Nicene Creed confesses, since the creed confesses a bodily, historical resurrection, a question treated as settled elsewhere in this map rather than reopened here.
positions.learn_detail: Some who hold this position intend it only for miracle accounts other than the resurrection, which they treat as a special, historically anchored case; others apply it consistently, including to the resurrection, which is where the position becomes contested rather than merely a matter of genre.

doctrines.learn_note: The affirmation that miracles are real divine acts and the recognition that scientific method cannot adjudicate them are compatible and usually held together; they are presented as separate positions here because they answer separate halves of the question this doctrine asks.

non-denominational.hold: Non-denominational evangelicals broadly affirm both that miracles are real, particular acts of God and that the scientific method, properly understood, is not equipped to rule them out; both convictions are usually held together rather than as competing options.
non-denominational.note: The two positions are compatible rather than rival for most in this stream; they are presented separately here because they answer different halves of the question the doctrine asks.
non-denominational.citation: National Association of Evangelicals, Statement of Faith; BioLogos, What We Believe

roman-catholic.hold: Miracles are affirmed as real divine acts and treated as motives of credibility for revelation, while the natural sciences are held, through a long engagement with them, to investigate natural causes only and so to be unable to adjudicate a miracle claim.
superseded_holds: Rome affirms miracles as real divine acts and treats them as motives of credibility for revelation, while also holding, through its long engagement with the natural sciences, that the scientific method properly investigates only natural causes and cannot itself adjudicate a miracle claim.
roman-catholic.note: Both convictions are held together rather than as competing options; the Pontifical Academy of Sciences has repeatedly distinguished methodological naturalism in scientific practice from a philosophical claim that nature is all there is.
roman-catholic.citation: First Vatican Council, Dei Filius, ch. 3 (1870); Pontifical Academy of Sciences, statements distinguishing methodological from philosophical naturalism
